prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B031 as my single preferred part, and the discussion has made the case firmer. The question of distinctness, which the chair put first, has a physical answer. The 2005 prize gave us the comb, a way to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize gave control of single quantum systems, which gave the best ion clocks. The lattice clock solved a different problem: holding thousands of neutral atoms in a trap that does not shift the clock transition. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes that light shift, and this is what made the stability and many-body regime reachable. It is an original experiment and an original idea, followed by verification in many independent laboratories (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) that agree at the 10^-18 level. It also opens a door: gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, tests of constants, dark-matter searches, and a redefinition of the second. The credit divides cleanly. Katori made the proposal and the first demonstrations, and Ye took the system to record accuracy and stability and to many-body clock physics. A citation that names magic-wavelength trapping states this precisely and keeps the prize from reading as a second frequency-comb prize.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain and I do not want to hide them. Novelty against the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a judgement, not a fact, and Mehlig, who ranks B031 eighth, has not yet said whether novelty is his only objection. The priority record is not fully verified from the supplied files: Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and the NIST and JILA teams made early lattice-clock demonstrations, and I am relying on memory that Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and 2003-2005 demonstrations precede them. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest application is prospective. Finally, B031 is an instrument as well as a physical idea, and I should apply the same standard to it that I applied to my own earlier first choice, B009. My answer is that B031 returns fundamental physics, while B009 as currently credited has the Krivanek priority question.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B024, built on a continuum-model prediction followed by the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, now with Bistritzer included in the theory credit, and concedes that B031 is the safer choice if maturity and attribution weigh more than novelty.
responses.response: I take the argument seriously. A prediction that was then confirmed by an unexpected experimental discovery is the pattern I respect, and eight years of replication across groups is a real record. My difficulty is the standard I keep returning to, that we must be absolutely sure the people credited did the original work. For B024 the first experimental author of the 2018 papers is outside every three-name credit, and Bistritzer's inclusion pushes out the experimental side rather than adding it. The pairing mechanism is also open, which means the citation has to be written so narrowly that it says little about the experiment. I would still keep B024 as my first alternative. I ask Mehlig to say plainly whether novelty alone puts B031 eighth, because I think the lattice-clock point above answers it, and whether he could accept B031 as a second choice.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that for B024 the theory-experiment link is what matters most, and that eight years of independent replication make the work no longer too young, while conceding that B031 is the safer and more mature choice if the pairing question and the attribution gap carry the room.
responses.response: I agree with the point about replication, and the 2010 graphene precedent is a good one. Where we differ is on whether the open pairing mechanism is a detail or a gap. For a prize about a discovery I would want the citation to rest on something that will not be rewritten, and flat bands and correlated insulators probably meet that standard, but the superconductivity, which was the headline in 2018, does not yet. I notice that Eriksson also names B031 as his alternative, and I would ask him to consider that the committee might wait for the pairing question to clear and then return to B024 with a clearer record. I do not think waiting weakens B024, since the discovery will not be lost to history in the meantime.

responses.point: Johansson supports B031 as a clean case of an original idea in which the magic-wavelength lattice precedes the accuracy regime, but lists the pending redefinition of the second and the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates as open uncertainties.
responses.response: I share both uncertainties. On the redefinition, I would not make the prize depend on it: the statutes ask for a discovery or invention that has been verified, and the verification is already in the record of cross-comparisons at the 10^-18 level. On priority, I cannot settle it from the supplied files and I do not want to pretend that I can. What I can say is that the first demonstrations at Tokyo and the accuracy programme at JILA are the two lines that the later groups built upon or confirmed. I would still ask that the chair or a colleague with the primary literature check the dates of the first lattice-clock spectroscopy before the final ballot, since that decides whether two names are right.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B005 to B031 but keeps B005 as his first alternative, and asks in his chair summary whether members who do not prefer B005 can state a rule that would let it be defended with three names.
responses.response: I cannot state such a rule, and I think that is the answer. Two reasonable rules, founding leadership or spokespeople at the time of the 2012 discovery, give different trios from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and four colleagues proposed three different trios. The science is beyond question and I would be glad to see the discovery recognised, but the committee cannot be absolutely sure it has named the right people under a three-person limit. That is why I list B005 only as an alternative and not as a preferred part. I also considered a second prize part and decided against it: B031 with B009 or B028 would need five or six names, which exceeds the limit, so I propose a single part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; I believe the magic-wavelength trapping step makes it so, but this is a judgement.

Priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Hinkley in the first lattice-clock demonstrations; I rely on memory and cannot verify it from the supplied files, and I ask for a record check before the final ballot.

Whether a precision-measurement instrument counts as a discovery or invention in the sense of the will; I think it does, given Ruska 1986 and the fundamental-physics return, but the committee should apply one standard to B031 and B009.
Whether the timing of the redefinition of the second, or the 2023, 2012 and 2005 atomic and optical prizes, should weigh against B031 this year.
statement.conflict_note: B009 lies directly in my own field and in the community I preside over (IFSM), so I would recuse myself from any discussion or vote on that candidate and I do not propose it in this configuration. For B031 I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025, where Katori is based, and I have long-running exchanges with the Tokyo microscopy community. This is a general institutional link and not a personal or collaborative one, and I do not consider it a conflict, but I record it. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, which does not bear on the candidates I discuss.
